sets.title: Dulce et Decorum Est
sets.author: Wilfred Owen
sets.source: Dulce et Decorum Est, in Poems (ed. Siegfried Sassoon), Chatto & Windus, 1920 (written 1917)
sets.headnote: Wilfred Owen was a British infantry officer who served on the Western Front and was killed in November 1918. He drafted this poem in 1917 after being treated for shell shock; it was published after his death. The Latin title and closing words come from the Roman poet Horace: it is sweet and fitting to die for one's country.
sets.body:
Bent double, like old beggars under sacks,
Knock-kneed, coughing like hags, we cursed through sludge,
Till on the haunting flares we turned our backs
And towards our distant rest began to trudge.
Men marched asleep. Many had lost their boots
But limped on, blood-shod. All went lame; all blind;
Drunk with fatigue; deaf even to the hoots
Of tired, outstripped Five-Nines that dropped behind.

Gas! GAS! Quick, boys!—An ecstasy of fumbling,
Fitting the clumsy helmets just in time;
But someone still was yelling out and stumbling,
And flound'ring like a man in fire or lime...
Dim, through the misty panes and thick green light,
As under a green sea, I saw him drowning.

In all my dreams, before my helpless sight,
He plunges at me, guttering, choking, drowning.

If in some smothering dreams you too could pace
Behind the wagon that we flung him in,
And watch the white eyes writhing in his face,
His hanging face, like a devil's sick of sin;
If you could hear, at every jolt, the blood
Come gargling from the froth-corrupted lungs,
Obscene as cancer, bitter as the cud
Of vile, incurable sores on innocent tongues,—
My friend, you would not tell with such high zest
To children ardent for some desperate glory,
The old Lie: Dulce et decorum est
Pro patria mori.

pair.title: The Soldier
pair.author: Rupert Brooke
pair.source: The Soldier, in 1914 and Other Poems, Sidgwick & Jackson, 1915
pair.headnote: Rupert Brooke wrote this sonnet in late 1914, early in the First World War, as the last of a sequence of five war sonnets. He died of illness on the way to Gallipoli in April 1915, before seeing combat.
pair.body:
If I should die, think only this of me:
That there's some corner of a foreign field
That is for ever England. There shall be
In that rich earth a richer dust concealed;
A dust whom England bore, shaped, made aware,
Gave, once, her flowers to love, her ways to roam,
A body of England's, breathing English air,
Washed by the rivers, blest by suns of home.

And think, this heart, all evil shed away,
A pulse in the eternal mind, no less
Gives somewhere back the thoughts by England given;
Her sights and sounds; dreams happy as her day;
And laughter, learnt of friends; and gentleness,
In hearts at peace, under an English heaven.

questions.model: In Text 1, Owen uses relentless sensory imagery to make the reader witness a death that patriotic rhetoric conceals. The attack erupts in broken exclamations, "Gas! GAS! Quick, boys!", whose capitals and fragments enact panic, while the oxymoron "An ecstasy of fumbling" captures a frenzy so intense it resembles a seizure. Visual imagery then distorts the scene: "Dim, through the misty panes and thick green light, / As under a green sea, I saw him drowning." Seen through the gas-mask lenses, the soldier appears to drown on dry land, and the present participle "drowning" leaves his death unfinished, a point reinforced when the word returns in the isolated couplet, "guttering, choking, drowning." In the final stanza Owen shifts to sound and texture: the reader is asked to "hear, at every jolt, the blood / Come gargling from the froth-corrupted lungs", and the similes "Obscene as cancer, bitter as the cud" make the death disgusting rather than noble. This assault on the senses is purposeful. Having made the reader see, hear and almost taste the death, Owen can expose the patriotic maxim as "The old Lie".

questions.text: In Text 2, explain how Brooke represents death in war as a gift to England.

criteria.descriptor: Provides a precise, well-reasoned explanation of how Brooke represents death in war as a gift to England, integrating well-chosen textual evidence and making the cause-and-effect relationship explicit
Provides a sound explanation of how Brooke represents death in war as a gift to England with appropriate textual reference

next_steps.0: Say directly how the speaker views his possible death, and quote the line about the "foreign field".
next_steps.1: Explain the idea of exchange: show how England gives to the speaker and how his death gives something back, using the sestet.
next_steps.2: Connect the imagery to tone: explain how the calm conditional opening and the peaceful final line make death seem a fulfilment rather than a sacrifice.

questions.model: Brooke represents the soldier's death not as loss but as an act of repayment and enrichment. The conditional opening "If I should die" calmly accepts death, and the speaker imagines his grave transforming "some corner of a foreign field" into territory "That is for ever England." His body becomes "a richer dust", the comparative implying that his burial improves the foreign soil. The death is framed as a return of what England gave: the nation "bore, shaped, made aware" him, and in the sestet his heart "Gives somewhere back the thoughts by England given." This cycle of giving and giving back casts dying as grateful repayment, and the closing image of "hearts at peace, under an English heaven" presents death as peaceful fulfilment rather than suffering.

questions.text: Compare how Text 1 and Text 2 represent the idea of dying for one's country.

Provides a thoughtful comparison of how the two poems represent dying for one's country, with relevant, analysed evidence from both texts

checklist: States a comparative thesis: Brooke idealises the death as a gift, Owen exposes the ideal as a lie
Contrasts the soldiers' bodies: "a richer dust" against "Bent double, like old beggars under sacks"
Compares form: Brooke's ordered sonnet against Owen's fractured stanzas and isolated couplet
Compares the address to the reader: "think only this of me" against "My friend, you would not tell"

next_steps.0: Write a thesis that names both poems' views on dying for one's country and how they differ.
next_steps.1: Support your thesis with one quotation from each poem that shows its view of the soldier.
next_steps.2: Analyse how language shapes each view, for example the purified dust in Text 2 against the grotesque "blood-shod" in Text 1.
next_steps.3: Compare a feature of form, such as Brooke's controlled sonnet against Owen's broken rhythm and isolated couplet, and explain what each structure suggests.
next_steps.4: Integrate your comparison: discuss both poems within each paragraph and compare how each speaker addresses the reader.
next_steps.5: Refine for Band 6: use context to explain why the poems differ, and conclude with a judgement about how reading them together sharpens each one.

questions.model:
Both poems ask the reader to contemplate death in war, but they reach opposite conclusions: Brooke idealises dying for England as a peaceful, meaningful gift, while Owen exposes that ideal as a lie told to the young.

The poems' representations of the soldier's body establish this contrast. Brooke's speaker addresses a loved reader with calm authority, "If I should die, think only this of me", and imagines his body as "A dust whom England bore, shaped, made aware", purified and absorbed into the nation. Owen's soldiers are instead "Bent double, like old beggars under sacks", a simile that strips them of youth and heroism, and they march "Drunk with fatigue". Where Brooke's body is "Washed by the rivers, blest by suns of home", Owen's men are "blood-shod", their suffering compressed into a grotesque compound.

Form reinforces the contrast. Brooke writes a composed sonnet whose regular rhyme and gentle iambic rhythm mirror the order of the speaker's faith, moving smoothly to "hearts at peace, under an English heaven." Owen opens with two stanzas that resemble a sonnet's octave but fractures the pattern: the frantic "Gas! GAS! Quick, boys!" breaks the rhythm, and an isolated couplet, "In all my dreams, before my helpless sight, / He plunges at me, guttering, choking, drowning", shows trauma refusing to settle into order.

Most pointedly, the poems differ in how they treat the reader. Brooke's imperative "think only this" limits what we may imagine, shielding civilians from the reality of combat. Owen does the reverse: "If you could hear, at every jolt, the blood / Come gargling from the froth-corrupted lungs" places the reader behind the wagon of the dying man. His bitter address, "My friend, you would not tell with such high zest / To children ardent for some desperate glory, / The old Lie", reads almost as a reply to poems like Brooke's.

Read together, the texts reveal how experience shapes representation. Brooke's sonnet imagines death before the trenches, while Owen, writing from them, insists that the dignity of "Dulce et decorum est" cannot survive the reality of a gas attack.

sets.title: Composed upon Westminster Bridge, September 3, 1802
sets.author: William Wordsworth
sets.source: Composed upon Westminster Bridge, September 3, 1802, in Poems, in Two Volumes, 1807
sets.headnote: William Wordsworth was an English Romantic poet. This Petrarchan sonnet records his view of London from Westminster Bridge early one morning in 1802.
sets.body:
Earth has not anything to show more fair:
Dull would he be of soul who could pass by
A sight so touching in its majesty:
This City now doth, like a garment, wear
The beauty of the morning; silent, bare,
Ships, towers, domes, theatres, and temples lie
Open unto the fields, and to the sky;
All bright and glittering in the smokeless air.
Never did sun more beautifully steep
In his first splendour, valley, rock, or hill;
Ne'er saw I, never felt, a calm so deep!
The river glideth at his own sweet will:
Dear God! the very houses seem asleep;
And all that mighty heart is lying still!

pair.title: London
pair.author: William Blake
pair.source: London, in Songs of Innocence and of Experience, 1794
pair.headnote: William Blake was a London poet, painter and engraver. This poem comes from Songs of Experience; the spelling and punctuation follow his engraved original.
pair.body:
I wander thro' each charter'd street,
Near where the charter'd Thames does flow,
And mark in every face I meet
Marks of weakness, marks of woe.

In every cry of every Man,
In every Infants cry of fear,
In every voice: in every ban,
The mind-forg'd manacles I hear

How the Chimney-sweepers cry
Every blackning Church appalls,
And the hapless Soldiers sigh
Runs in blood down Palace walls

But most thro' midnight streets I hear
How the youthful Harlots curse
Blasts the new-born Infants tear
And blights with plagues the Marriage hearse

questions.model: The speaker regards the sleeping city with awe and reverent wonder. This attitude is conveyed through personification and simile: the city "doth, like a garment, wear / The beauty of the morning", so London is imagined as a figure clothed in natural beauty rather than as a place of industry. The garment image also implies the beauty is temporary, put on only for the dawn, which deepens the speaker's wonder at seeing it "silent, bare".

questions.model: In Text 2, Blake represents London's suffering as universal, systemic and partly self-imposed. The speaker's wandering reveals a city that is owned and controlled: the repetition of "charter'd" for both the streets and "the charter'd Thames" suggests that even nature has been bought and regulated. The pun in "mark in every face I meet / Marks of weakness, marks of woe" turns the act of noticing into a kind of branding, as though misery has been stamped on every citizen. In the second stanza the anaphora of "In every" builds a relentless catalogue that culminates in "The mind-forg'd manacles I hear", a metaphor suggesting that people are chained by accepted ideas as much as by the powerful. Blake then links private misery to public institutions: the "Chimney-sweepers cry" shames the "blackning Church", and the soldier's sigh "Runs in blood down Palace walls", a synaesthetic image that turns a sound into a stain of guilt. The final oxymoron "Marriage hearse" shows suffering infecting even the beginning of new life, so the city's misery appears inescapable.

next_steps.0: Write a thesis that states how each poem represents London and the key difference between them.
next_steps.1: Support your thesis with a quotation from each text and explain what each reveals about the city.
next_steps.2: Compare the speakers' perspectives: where each stands, what each looks at, and how that shapes what they see.
next_steps.3: Compare a feature of form or sound in both poems and explain how it reinforces each representation.

questions.model:
Both poems view London through a single speaker, but Wordsworth presents a transcendent, idealised city at rest, while Blake exposes a city of institutional cruelty and human pain.

Wordsworth's speaker is still and elevated, surveying the scene from the bridge, and his hyperbolic opening, "Earth has not anything to show more fair", frames the city as a natural wonder. Its buildings, "Ships, towers, domes, theatres, and temples", lie "Open unto the fields, and to the sky", so the city merges with nature in "the smokeless air". Blake's speaker, by contrast, moves "thro' each charter'd street" at ground level and sees people rather than buildings, finding "Marks of weakness, marks of woe" in every face.

Form and sound reinforce these contrasts. Wordsworth's Petrarchan sonnet builds to exclamations of wonder, "Dear God! the very houses seem asleep", and its long vowels slow the reader into the calm the speaker feels. Blake's short quatrains and insistent repetition of "every" create a claustrophobic, hammering rhythm, and his images of the "blackning Church" and "Palace walls" bring institutions into a city that Wordsworth presents only as architecture.

Significantly, Wordsworth's London is beautiful precisely because it is empty and silent: "all that mighty heart is lying still!" Blake's London is defined by human noise, by "the youthful Harlots curse" heard through "midnight streets". Read together, the texts suggest that the idealised city exists only while its people sleep, whereas Blake insists that the reader hear them.

sets.title: The Drover's Wife (extract)
sets.author: Henry Lawson
sets.source: The Drover's Wife, in While the Billy Boils, Angus & Robertson, 1896 (first published in The Bulletin, 1892)
sets.headnote: Henry Lawson was an Australian writer of stories and verse about bush life in the 1890s. This is the opening of his short story about a woman left alone with her children on an isolated selection.
sets.body:
The two-roomed house is built of round timber, slabs, and stringy-bark, and floored with split slabs. A big bark kitchen standing at one end is larger than the house itself, veranda included.

Bush all round—bush with no horizon, for the country is flat. No ranges in the distance. The bush consists of stunted, rotten native apple-trees. No undergrowth. Nothing to relieve the eye save the darker green of a few she-oaks which are sighing above the narrow, almost waterless creek. Nineteen miles to the nearest sign of civilization—a shanty on the main road.

The drover, an ex-squatter, is away with sheep. His wife and children are left here alone.

Four ragged, dried-up-looking children are playing about the house. Suddenly one of them yells: 'Snake! Mother, here's a snake!'

The gaunt, sun-browned bushwoman dashes from the kitchen, snatches her baby from the ground, holds it on her left hip, and reaches for a stick.

'Where is it?'

'Here! gone into the wood-heap!' yells the eldest boy—a sharp-faced urchin of eleven. 'Stop there, mother! I'll have him. Stand back! I'll have the beggar!'

'Tommy, come here, or you'll be bit. Come here at once when I tell you, you little wretch!'

The youngster comes reluctantly, carrying a stick bigger than himself. Then he yells, triumphantly: 'There it goes—under the house!' and darts away with club uplifted. At the same time the big, black, yellow-eyed dog-of-all-breeds, who has shown the wildest interest in the proceedings, breaks his chain and rushes after that snake. He is a moment late, however, and his nose reaches the crack in the slabs just as the end of its tail disappears. Almost at the same moment the boy's club comes down and skins the aforesaid nose. Alligator takes small notice of this, and proceeds to undermine the building; but he is subdued after a struggle and chained up. They cannot afford to lose him.

pair.title: The Chosen Vessel (extract)
pair.author: Barbara Baynton
pair.source: The Chosen Vessel, in Bush Studies, Duckworth, 1902
pair.headnote: Barbara Baynton was an Australian writer whose collection Bush Studies presents a darker view of bush life than many writers of her time. This is the opening paragraph of her story about a young mother on a remote selection.
pair.body: She laid the stick and her baby on the grass while she untied the rope that tethered the calf. The length of the rope separated them. The cow was near the calf, and both were lying down. Feed along the creek was plentiful, and every day she found a fresh place to tether it, since tether it she must, for if she did not, it would stray with the cow out on the plain. She had plenty of time to go after it, but then there was baby; and if the cow turned on her out on the plain, and she with baby,—she had been a town girl and was afraid of the cow, but she did not want the cow to know it. She used to run at first when it bellowed its protest against the penning up of its calf. This satisfied the cow, also the calf, but the woman's husband was angry, and called her—the noun was cur. It was he who forced her to run and meet the advancing cow, brandishing a stick, and uttering threatening words till the enemy turned and ran. 'That's the way!' the man said, laughing at her white face. In many things he was worse than the cow, and she wondered if the same rule would apply to the man, but she was not one to provoke skirmishes even with the cow.

questions.model: Lawson presents the setting as harsh, monotonous and isolating, so that the reader understands the bushwoman's life as one of endurance without support. The opening uses a flat, inventory-like style, "The two-roomed house is built of round timber, slabs, and stringy-bark", and the present tense makes the scene feel permanent rather than passing. Minor sentences such as "No ranges in the distance." and "No undergrowth." build a pattern of negation that defines the landscape by what it lacks, and the bush stretches with "no horizon, for the country is flat", an enclosure with no visible escape. Even the trees are "stunted, rotten native apple-trees", adjectives of decay and restricted growth that parallel the family's poverty, while the she-oaks "sighing above the narrow, almost waterless creek" lend the scene a mournful tone. Isolation is measured precisely: "Nineteen miles to the nearest sign of civilization", and that sign proves to be merely "a shanty on the main road", a deflating anticlimax. Against this setting the plain sentence "His wife and children are left here alone" carries great weight, so when the snake appears the reader understands that she must face danger with only her children and a dog.

questions.model: Baynton presents the marriage as one of contempt and intimidation, in which the husband's cruelty exceeds any threat from the land. When the woman runs from the bellowing cow, her husband is angry and insults her: the narrator's detached aside, "the noun was cur", withholds the insult until the end of the sentence, so the single word lands like a blow and reduces her to an animal. His mockery is also physical, as he laughs "at her white face", finding amusement in her fear. The narrator's ironic comparison, "In many things he was worse than the cow", then makes the threat explicit, and her wondering whether "the same rule would apply to the man" suggests she must constantly calculate how to manage him. The relationship is one of fear disguised as everyday routine.

questions.model:
Read together, the two extracts suggest that a bushwoman's life is defined by isolation, constant vigilance and a strength that goes unrecognised, but they differ in where they locate the greatest threat: Lawson in the land, Baynton in the man.

In Text 1 the husband's absence is stated flatly: "The drover, an ex-squatter, is away with sheep. His wife and children are left here alone." The verb "left" hints at abandonment, and when the snake appears the woman acts at once: she "snatches her baby from the ground, holds it on her left hip, and reaches for a stick." The string of urgent verbs presents her competence as instinctive, a habit forged by necessity. Baynton's woman also carries a stick and "her baby", but her courage is coerced. She "had been a town girl and was afraid of the cow", and it is her husband "who forced her to run and meet the advancing cow, brandishing a stick".

The texts also differ in perspective. Lawson's present-tense narration is sympathetic but external; he calls her "The gaunt, sun-browned bushwoman", a description that shows how the land has shaped her body. Baynton stays closer to the woman's mind, and her irony is darker: the remark that "In many things he was worse than the cow" reveals that the real danger is human. Even fear must be hidden, since "she did not want the cow to know it", a detail suggesting she has learned to conceal weakness from every creature around her, including her husband.

Synthesising these perspectives, the extracts complicate the masculine bush legend of the 1890s. Lawson honours the woman's endurance against a hostile environment, while Baynton exposes the domestic cruelty that the legend overlooks. Together they suggest that the bushwoman's courage is real, but that it is demanded of her by isolation, by danger and by men, rather than freely chosen.
